title: Bidirectional A*: Lisbon to the fastest route!
description: Watch Bidirectional A* slice through a real street-map graph from both ends, shrinking the search space fast. The visualization shows two expanding frontiers meeting in the middle to produce an efficient shortest path.
ig_caption:
🗺️🚦 Lisbon’s Parque das Nações, but make it algorithmic. 

In this reel, **Bidirectional A*** runs two informed searches on the same street-map graph: one from the start node and one from the goal node. Each side uses the A* idea—**f(n) = g(n) + h(n)**—where **g(n)** tracks actual travel cost along streets and **h(n)** estimates remaining distance to the opposite frontier using a heuristic (e.g., straight-line distance). ✨

🧠 Why it’s cool: on large real-world grids/road graphs, expanding from *both ends* often cuts the number of explored nodes dramatically. In graph-theory terms, we’re doing **heuristic-driven shortest-path search on a weighted graph**, and the solution emerges when the two search trees/frontiers **intersect** (meeting condition). 

📍Edges represent road segments; nodes represent intersections/turn points. The moment you see the two waves connect, you’ve essentially pinpointed the shortest route under the chosen weights and heuristic.

yt_description:
Lisbon (Parque das Nações) street-map pathfinding using **Bidirectional A***! Watch two heuristic searches expand from start and goal, then meet in the middle to reduce explored nodes. 

✅ Keywords: Bidirectional A* visualization, A* pathfinding, shortest path, graph search, real-world street maps, coding algorithms, computerscience.

🎬 Mechanics: The map is converted into a weighted graph (intersections as nodes, road segments as edges). Each search uses f(n)=g(n)+h(n), and the final route is reconstructed when the frontiers intersect.
